title: DOMAIN-SPECIFIC MODEL FOR SURFACING HIGH-SURPRISAL INFORMATION
technical_field: The present disclosure relates generally to natural language processing and, more specifically, to methods and systems for identifying and surfacing high-surprisal information within textual data.
background_art: The volume of data that is created by humans has grown at a rate of 54% per year over the last decade. Ninety percent of this data is unstructured data, and much of that unstructured data is in the form of narrative text.
summary_of_invention: According to embodiments of the present disclosure, methods of and computer program products for surfacing high-surprisal information are provided. In some embodiments, a method of surfacing high-surprisal information includes reading an input document. The input document can comprise an ordered sequence of tokens. In some embodiments, the method includes, for each token of the ordered sequence of tokens, generating by a language model a probability distribution of predicted tokens based on preceding tokens in the ordered sequence. In some embodiments, the method includes comparing each token to its predicted tokens to determine a probability of occurrence of that token. In some embodiments, the method includes, based on the probability of occurrence of each token, assigning a surprise value thereto.

detailed_description:
With the growth of the volume of content over recent years, identifying information that is relevant within text data remains a challenge. It would be desirable for an automated system to identify information that is new in a given document relative to a set of known information. In some embodiments, the present disclosure provides a language model such as a large language model (LLM) that determines new or surprising information within textual data. In some embodiments, a domain-neutral LLM is trained on a corpus of data from a plurality of domains, and a domain-specific LLM is trained on a target domain. Once trained, the LLM can identify new or surprising information in any new document or narrative disclosure.

Training a Domain-Neutral Model
FIG. 1A is a block diagram 100 of an LLM Model Factory 112 training a domain-neutral model 108. In some embodiments, the domain-neutral model 108 is a language model such as a large language model (LLM). In some embodiments, the domain-neutral LLM 108 is trained on a corpus of documents 102. The corpus of documents 102 can be categorized into multiple domains 104a-e. Each of the multiple domains 104a-e includes multiple documents 106.

In some embodiment, a domain (e.g., domains 104a-e) can refer to a company, a corporation, an enterprise, an industry, a firm, an author, a periodical, a type of document (e.g., a contract, a license, a sales agreement, a purchase agreement, legislation), a subject-matter category, a source of the document, or other categorization of document.

In some embodiments, the documents 106 include unstructured text data. In some embodiments, the documents 106 include narrative disclosures. In some embodiments, the documents 106 are in the category of their respective domain 104a-e. For example, if domain 104a is the company Apple®, the documents 106 can be relating to that company. In some embodiments, the domains 104a-e are each a respective company. In some embodiments, each company is a company in a financial market. In some embodiments, the documents 106 can include corporate disclosures such as filings before the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) (e.g., Form 10-Q, Form 10-K, Form 8-K), or press releases of a company, etc.).

In some embodiments, the corpus of documents 102 are pre-processed to remove numerical data, such as tables. In some embodiments, the pre-processing focuses the training of the model 108 on the narrative content. In some embodiments, the pre-processing tokenizes the training data.

In some embodiments, a tokenizer can convert text into tokens and can encode the tokens as vectors for both training and use of the models. In some embodiments, the tokenizer is separate from the large language model and provides its output (e.g., an ordered sequence of tokens) to one or more large language model as training data or inference data. In some embodiments, the tokenizer can be considered part of the large language model. In some embodiments, the tokenizer can be applied to training documents, inference documents, or both.

While tokens can be based upon entire words (e.g., each full word being a unique token), however, tokenizing in such a way leads to a large vocabulary. In some embodiments, sub-piece or sub-word tokens can be employed because many words are constructed by combining sub-pieces together. For example, some sub-pieces may share meaning across the vocabulary (e.g., the prefix "un" in words such as unpresumptuous and unselfish).

Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) can leverage commonality across words to build a vocabulary of a more manageable size. BPE can find a smaller number of unique sub-words in the corpus, along with individual characters (e.g., symbols) that can be used to form the words in the target vocabulary. BPE can merge pairs of adjacent individual characters/symbols which are most commonly found next to one another and can iterate this process until the vocabulary is reduced to a target size.

In some embodiments, a tokenizer is trained starting from a blank model (e.g., from scratch) using the disclosures within the corpus. In some embodiments, where the disclosures of the corpus are divided into in-sample training data (e.g., training data 202 of FIG. 2) and "out of sample" inference data (e.g., inference data 204 of FIG. 2), the tokenizer can be only trained on the in-sample training data. In some embodiments, the inputs to the training process include tokens for the Arabic numerals 0, 1, ... 9. In some embodiments, this results in a tokenizer with a vocabulary size of about 50,270. In some embodiments, the vocabluary size represents the number of tokens learned via the training process, the ten Arabic numeral tokens, and three special tokens for beginning of sentence, end of sentence, and unknown (word that is not in the vocabulary).

In some embodiments, the documents of the corpus of documents 102 include timestamps representing a time of creation or time of publication of each document.

In some embodiments, the LLM Model Factory 112 trains a domain-neutral model 108 on the corpus of documents 102. In some embodiments, the LLM Model Factory 112 initializes the training with an default model 114. In some embodiments, the LLM Model Factory 112 initializes the training by setting the parameters of the domain-neutral model 108 to be trained to random non-zero values. In some embodiments, the LLM Model Factory 112 initializes the training by providing the default model 114 (e.g., a blank model) having parameters as random non-zero values. In some embodiments, after training, the domain-neutral model 108 includes domain-neutral parameters 110.

In some embodiments, the domain-neutral model is trained from a blank model or model with randomly assigned weights (e.g., from scratch) on unstructured text data (e.g., historical narrative data, historical information, financial disclosures) contained in 2,.

In some embodiments, a domain-neutral model is trained on a corpus, such as the narrative content extracted from the disclosures of all firms in sample filed on EDGAR from 1996 through the end of 2006. In some embodiments, the training data includes 22.8 GB of narrative content and more than 3.6 billion words.

In some embodiments, the filings gathered from the EDGAR database can contain a mix of narrative and quantitative content, such as tabular financial statements. In some embodiments, narrative content is extracted from the filings. In some embodiments, the method used to extract narrative content varies based on whether the file type of the narrative content is plain text or HTML.

In some embodiments, plain text filings and attachments-which are systematically older filings on average-often contain standardized general markup language (SGML) tags. In some embodiments, these tags can identify special content (e.g., tabular content) and render the special content in a more human-readable format based on the capabilities of the system used to view the content (e.g., a personal computer versus a Bloomberg Terminal). In some embodiments, these tags can identify tabular quantitative content in plain text filings and remove such tabular quantitative content.

In some embodiments, HTML filings and attachments use tables to structure content (e.g., present a graph on one half of the page while typesetting narrative content on the other half). In some embodiments, this increases the difficulty of removing tabular quantitative content. In some embodiments, the number of characters as rendered by a web browser per HTML tag is measured (CPT). Content is removed where more than a threshold percentage of the CPT measure are numbers. In some embodiments, content of HTML tags having a text density below a threshold are removed.

In some embodiments, a CPT threshold of 10 is used to identify narrative content embedded in HTML tables. In some embodiments, when the number of non-numeric, non-blank, and non-punctuation characters per tag in a given table exceeds 10, the narrative content is extracted from the table, and the content of the table is ignored or removed from the document.

After removing tables having a CPT less than 10, the text is extracted from the remaining HTML while preserving meaningful formatting such as indentation and line breaks. In some embodiments, this provides a corpus of documents 102 (e.g., a corpus of plain text documents) that are structurally similar regardless of source file type or the time period when the form was filed.

In some embodiments, the domain-neutral model is trained by randomly initializing the parameters 0, and training the domain-neutral model on the corpus for 10 epochs. In some embodiments, the training can be for more or less than 10 epochs. However, after 10 epochs, further training may only marginally the objective evaluated on an out-of-sample data set.

Training a Domain-Specific Model
FIG. 1B is a block diagram 130 of an LLM Model Factory 112 training a domain-specific model 132. In some embodiments, the LLM Model Factory 112 trains a domain-specific model 132 for a target domain 138 (e.g., Domain 104a). In some embodiments, the domain-specific model 132 is a language model such as a large language model. In some embodiments, the target domain 138 can be any of the domains 104a-e used to train the domain-neutral model 108. In some embodiments, the target domain 138 can be a domain other than the domains 104a-e used to train the domain-neutral model 108.

In some embodiments, the LLM Model Factory 112 trains the domain-specific model 132 based on documents 136 from the target domain 138. In some embodiments, the target domain 138 can be one of the domains 104a-e used to train the domain-specific model. In such a case, the documents 136 can be the same documents 106 used to train the domain-neutral model 108 for that domain 104a-e or the documents 136 can be different in whole or in part from the documents 106 used to train the domain neutral model 108 for that domain 104a-e.

In some embodiments, the target domain 138 can be a domain different than any of the domains 104a-e. In such a case, the documents 136 can be different, at least in part, from the documents 106 used to train the domain-neutral model 108. In some embodiments, the documents 106 associated with the target domain 138 include timestamps.

In alternative approaches, fine-tuned models are based on a first model pre-trained on the entire corpus, including inference data. In contrast to these alternative approaches, some embodiments of the domain-neutral model 108 train on historical narrative data that is separate from the inference data.

In some embodiments, the LLM Model Factory 112 trains the domain-specific model 132 based on the documents 136 of the target domain 138. In some embodiments, the LLM Model Factory 112 initializes said training with domain-neutral parameters 110 from the domain-neutral model 108. In some embodiments, once trained, the domain-specific model 132 includes domain-specific parameters 134.

In some embodiments, the LLM Model Factory 112 trains a plurality of domain-specific model, each domain-specific model trained based on one of the domains 104a-e. In some embodiments, the training of the plurality of domain-specific models results in a domain-specific model for each domain 104a-e that was used to train the domain-neutral model 108.

In some embodiments, once trained, the domain-specific LLM detects new information in an input document.

In some embodiments, the domain-specific model 132 is configured to provide an estimate for a specific domain, such as a firm or company, of prior beliefs that can be used to compute a measure of information, such as high-surprisal information. In some embodiments, high-surprisal information is content having a low probability of occurring given a context. A domain-specific model 132 is trained to estimate such prior beliefs by being initialized with domain-neutral parameters 110 of the domain-neutral model 108 and being trained on the target domain 138 (e.g., fine-tuning).

In some embodiments, a separate domain-specific model 132 can be generated for each domain 104a-e illustrated by FIG. 1A. The set of domains (e.g., firms) can be indexed by F=1, 2, ..., p. The set of indices associated with disclosures in the domain f before time t can be represented by Jft. The firm-specific information set at time t for firm f can be approximated by P(D|Jft). In some embodiments, the domain-neutral model and domain-specific model 132 can then train the domain-neutral model 108 on the corpus of documents 102.

In some embodiments, the domain-specific model 132 is trained on a corpus of documents, which can include a set of narrative disclosures (e.g., documents) in a plain text format. In some embodiments, in a financial example, the narrative disclosures are gathered from the SEC EDGAR database. Notably, EDGAR system can accept and disseminate a wide array of filings, ranging from lengthy annual reports (e.g., Form 10-K) to brief and standardized disclosures such as changes in beneficial ownership (e.g., Form 4). In some embodiments, the corpus could include all such disclosures on EDGAR. In some embodiments, the corpus includes documents having narrative disclosures (e.g., those that primarily contain length written-word content, those having unstructured textual data) measuring the information in narrative disclosures.

In some embodiments, the three most voluminous form types are the Current Report (e.g., Form 8-K), Quarterly Report (e.g., Form 10-Q), and Annual Report (e.g., Form 10-K), respectively. Table 2, below, presents the volume of narrative disclosure filed on the SEC's EDGAR system from 1996 through 2022 by form type for the 20 longest form types based on word count.

In some embodiments, the domain-specific model 132 can be trained on documents from a target company. Such training can model beliefs over narrative content. This domain-specific model can be then used to identify new information that the target company communicates.

In some embodiments, the domain-specific model is a large language model that can generate text in response to an input prompt, such as an ordered sequence of tokens. In some embodiments, the domain-neutral model and domain-specific model a probability distribution of expected text given a prompt. In some embodiments, the probability distribution can be a probability of a next predicted token given preceding tokens in the ordered sequence of tokens.

Therefore, providing a prompt to the domain-neutral model 108 of FIG. 1A can cause the respective model(s) to generate text output based on the prompt. FIG. 3 is a representation of document 300 having variably highlighted sentences. In some embodiments, the domain-specific model 132 of FIGS. 1B-C can output a measure of high-surprisal information for a given prediction window. The prediction window can be a token, word, sentence, paragraph, or other size. The measure of high-surprisal information for the prediction window can combine the measures of high surprisal information (e.g., the surprise value 170 of FIG. 1C) for each token in the prediction window. In some embodiments, such as an embodiment illustrated by FIG. 3, the prediction window is a sentence.

In some embodiments, the shade of the highlighting of each prediction window is proportional to the combined measure of high-surprisal information. That combined measure of high-surprisal information can represent the domain-specific model's 132 estimate of new information in that prediction window. The estimate of new information can represent high-surprisal information relative to the training data 202 (e.g., Apple-specific prior of pre-2007 information).

In some embodiments and with reference to FIG. 3, the document being analyzed is an announcement dated Jan. 17, 2007, disclosed in Apple's 8-K filing, where the company first mentions the introduction of its iPhone. While the disclosure contains numerous pieces of information, such as record revenue, the sentence illustrated as having the most inforation-according to the estimated prior is the sentence in which Apple mentions launching the iPhone and Apple TV.

FIG. 4 are graphs 400, 420, and 440 representing an information metric as a function of position in the document. In some embodiments, the model can be validated by examining the location of information in 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K filings uncovered by the surprise value in a financial example. For each filing, the body of the filing (e.g., the portion of the filing that generally follows a standardized format prescribed by the SEC) can be considered separately from exhibits. In some embodiments, the token-by-token information is computed using the respective prior. In some embodiments, the position of each token is normalized in the filing such that the first token corresponds to a position marked by 0%, and the last token corresponds to 100%.

In some embodiments, a geometric mean of the measure of high-surprisal information can be calculated within each percent increment of the document (e.g., [0%, 1%], [1%, 2%], [99%, 100%]). In some embodiments, other increments can be used to calculate the geometric mean of the surprise value. In some embodiments, when a given filing has multiple exhibits, then the exhibits can be combined by computing the arithmetic mean of the measure of high-surprisal information for each percentage increment across exhibits, weighted by the length of each exhibit. In some embodiments, the means are then averaged across all filings to determine common locations in each document time that contain high-surprisal information.

Each respective graph 400, 420, and 440 illustrates the main filing and exhibits with separate lines, as indicated by the legend 450. The graph 400 representing 10-K filings and the graph 440 representing 8-K filings illustrate that exhibits can be more informative than the main filing. However, the graph 420 representing the 10-Q filings illustrates that the main filings can be more informative than the exhibits. Across all filing types, the graphs 400, 420, and 440 illustrate that high-surprisal information can spike toward the end of the filing. In some cases, for 10-K/Q filings, the high-surprisal information spike may be driven by footnotes or endnotes. For 8-K forms, graph 440 illustrates that the high-surprisal information spike can be largest in the exhibits. In some cases, this may be because firms provide boilerplate information in the beginning of documents, (e.g., caveats to forward-looking statements) followed by more detailed information at the end of the documents (e.g., a discussion of new business strategies).

Table 8A presents example results from estimating Equation 7 for annual reports, and Table 8B presents example results for estimating Equation 7 for quarterly reports. In the examples analyzed by Tables 8A-B, across all measures and form types, there is evidence of statistically and economically significant market reactions on the disclosure event day. For example, estimates of ẞ₁ for AbsoluteReturn range from 0.465 to 1.190 with t-stats ranging from 12.17 to 18.08. These estimates can represent an economically significant 22.8% to 58.6% increase in AbsoluteReturn relative to the sample mean. Moving from the lowest to the highest decile of Info measure can be associated with a highly statistically and economically significant market reaction. For example, columns (3) and (6) in Table 8B indicate the corresponding 71.4% and 143% increases in AbsoluteReturn and Volume, respectively. Further, estimates of ẞ₁ can shrink considerably, such as in columns (3) and (6)) because they represent just 23.0% and 33.0% increases, respectively, versus 58.6% and 104% in columns (1) and (4), respectively. In contrast, examining the Length benchmark as a measure of information, results can be inconsistent (t-stats range from -1.853 to 4.283).

Collectively, the example evidence of Tables 9A-B highlights the importance of measuring information in the textual data to understand the sentiment. Alternative methods of examining solely 10-K filings find a roughly 25 bps spread between the extreme quintiles of negative sentiment, which is confirmed and validated by the results of embodiments of the models and LLMs disclosed herein. However, when accounting for the interaction between information and sentiment, (e.g., considering sentiment over the informative portion of the document) the effect shown by the example data is more than an order of magnitude greater, (e.g., between 318.7 and 524.5 basis points). This is consistent with the notion that (i) the measure can capture the information in narrative content rather than some other latent time-varying firm characteristic, and (ii) the sentiment of non-informative content should not influence prices.

In some embodiments, additional tests examine the extent to which the measure of information in textual disclosures can be predictive of future firm fundamental performance. The the following model can provide a measure of firm performance:

Equation 9 can define a predictive regression regarding the value of yf.q+t based solely on information available in quarter q. For analysis of annual and quarterly reports, the Form 10-K/Q filing over which information is computed comes out some time after q but generally before q+1. In that sense, the data required to make predictions were not available until some time after q but before q+1. As a result, introducing a time-invariant fixed effect into the regression is inappropriate since doing so requires foresight into future realizations. For this reason, two versions of Equation 9 are estimated: (a) a levels specification and (b) a differences specification. In some embodiments, a benefit of the difference specification is that any time-invariant firm characteristics, which may be responsible for firm perfor- mance, are differenced out.

Specifically, one, two, three, and four years later, the relation is associated with 8.3%, 6.0%, 4.6%, and 4.2% increases in ROA, respectively.

For current reports, there a similar but smaller pattern can be observed. FIG. 15 is a flowchart 1500 illustrating a method of uncovering high-surprisal information according to embodiments of the present disclosure. In some embodiments, a domain-specific large language model (e.g., domain-specific model 132 of FIG. 1C) reads an input document having an ordered sequence of tokens 1502. In some embodiments, the input document is processed by a tokenizer to generate the ordered sequence of tokens. For each token of the ordered sequence of tokens, the domain-specific large language model can generate a probability distribution of predicted tokens based on preceding tokens in the ordered sequence 1504. The domain-specific model can compare each token to its predicted tokens to determine a probability of occurrence of that token 1506. The domain-specific model can assign a surprise value based on the occurrence of each token 1508.

In some embodiments, the surprise value of each token can be averaged or combined with other tokens to provide a combined surprise value at the word, phrase, sentence, paragraph, section, or document level.

FIG. 16 is a flowchart 1600 illustrating a method of training a model to uncover high-surprisal information. A model training factory (e.g., LLM training factory 112 of FIGS. 1A-B) can read a corpus of documents 1602. Each document in the corpus can be associated with a domain. The model training factory can train a domain-neutral large language model on the corpus 1604. The model training factory can further generate a domain-specific large language model based on the domain-neutral large language model for a target domain 1606.

In some embodiments, optionally, the model training factory can determine whether additional models should be trained for more target domains, such as the domains associated with documents in the corpus 1608. If so, the model training factory generates a domain-specific large language model for the next target domain 1606. This optional process can iterate until there are no more target domain to generate a domain-specific model and model training is complete 1610.

abstract: A method of surfacing high-surprisal information includes reading an input document. The input document can comprise an ordered sequence of tokens. The method includes, for each token of the ordered sequence of tokens, generating by a language model a probability distribution of predicted tokens based on preceding tokens in the ordered sequence. The method includes comparing each token to its predicted tokens to determine a probability of occurrence of that token. The method includes, based on the probability of occurrence of each token, assigning a surprise value thereto.
